title: Writing and Learning for Democracy
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by a reader's request for a case for writing instruction that rests on democracy rather than employment, Stuart argues that the civic rationale is the part of the case schools have let go quiet. He sets it up through a theology teacher troubled by students asking when they will use this, careful to note that the man was not dismissing the need for value but worried about a purely utilitarian account of education. Stuart grants utility its place, he wants his own children able to earn a living, then insists it is far from the whole. The civic claim is stated bluntly: students must build knowledge, argue, read, write, speak and listen with increasing skill because the republic depends on their being capable by eighteen. He sets this against a list of culturally ascendant ME-exalting messages, do what makes you happy, each person decides what is right for them. His pedagogical point is practical and defuses the obvious objection: evidence-based reasoning need not be practised on hot-button issues, and in his own classroom rarely is, because clear thinking is hard when emotions are close at hand. Quoting Willingham, he argues the reachable audience is not the marcher but the thousands who read and half-agree.
points: The argument relocates the case for literacy from employability to citizenship, while explicitly granting utility its place rather than dismissing it.
The pedagogical move is the practically important one: evidence-and-reasoning habits are built on ordinary curricular questions, not on hot-button issues where emotion crowds out clear thinking.
Stuart supplies the actual sentence frames, this is the best way to solve that problem because, which makes the habit teachable in maths and science as much as in English.
The Willingham passage reframes the target audience, arguing the reachable people are not the committed but the many who read and think they see the point.
The closing section takes the harder position, that refusing to teach moral knowledge leaves students as their own arbiters and forfeits the right to complain about where they land.
quotes: Utility is part of the rationale for an education — I want my daughters and son to be able to earn a living for themselves and their families — but, just like the professor in California was getting at, it is far from the whole.

we need our students to build knowledge, argue, read, write, speak, and listen frequently and with ever greater care and skill because our democratic republic depends on them being knowledgeable and skillful in these areas by the time they're 18.
You ought to become a thoughtful, literate person not just because of what it can do for your life, but because of what it can do for all of our lives.

The public school classroom never ought to be used to teach one's political or religious views as the only way, but it always ought to be a place where we teach and require students to found opinions on strong evidence and clear reasoning.
Like Mr. Miagi asking Daniel to “wax on, wax off,” what we're doing here is building an unconscious bias toward reasoned decision-making.
It is a harsh thing, I think, to fail to equip our young people with the moral knowledge that humans have accrued over the centuries.
